subsections.subsection_title: 1. What the OSCE station may say

blocks.title: You may encounter any of the following:

items.text: Emergency assessment: A 26-year-old woman presents with sudden severe lower abdominal pain. Assess her and outline your immediate management.
Focused history: Take a focused history from a woman presenting with acute pelvic pain.
Clinical examination: Examine a patient with lower abdominal pain and report your findings.
Pregnancy-related emergency: A woman with pelvic pain and vaginal bleeding has a positive pregnancy test. Discuss your differential diagnoses and initial management.
Investigation interpretation: Interpret a pelvic ultrasound showing an adnexal mass and free fluid.
Differential diagnosis: Differentiate ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, a ruptured ovarian cyst, pelvic inflammatory disease and appendicitis.
Communication station: Explain to a patient why urgent investigation or surgery may be necessary.

blocks.text: Acute pelvic pain is pain arising in the lower abdomen or pelvis that develops suddenly or over a short period and may require urgent assessment.
In a patient of reproductive potential, acute pelvic pain must be approached systematically because some causes are life-threatening or can result in loss of fertility.
1. Pregnancy-related causes
Ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage and complications of pregnancy.
2. Gynaecological causes
Ovarian torsion, ruptured or haemorrhagic ovarian cyst, pelvic inflammatory disease, endometriosis-related pain and fibroid degeneration.
3. Gastrointestinal causes
Appendicitis, gastroenteritis, bowel obstruction, inflammatory bowel disease and constipation.
4. Urinary causes
Urinary tract infection, pyelonephritis, ureteric colic and urinary retention.
Before taking a detailed history, determine whether the patient is stable.

items.text: Hypotension, tachycardia or signs of shock.
Syncope or severe dizziness.
Severe, rapidly worsening pain.
Guarding, rebound tenderness or generalized peritonism.
Positive pregnancy test with pelvic pain, especially with bleeding.
Shoulder-tip pain with abdominal pain or collapse.
Heavy vaginal bleeding.
Fever with severe pelvic pain or signs of sepsis.
Persistent vomiting or a suspected surgical abdomen.

blocks.text: OSCE rule: If the patient is unstable, begin resuscitation and call for urgent senior help. Do not delay treatment to complete a history or wait for ultrasound.
A — Airway
Assess whether the airway is patent and whether the patient can speak normally.
B — Breathing
Assess respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and work of breathing. Give oxygen if clinically indicated.
C — Circulation
Check pulse, blood pressure, capillary refill, peripheral temperature and signs of blood loss. Establish IV access and initiate resuscitation when indicated.
D — Disability
Assess consciousness, confusion and pain severity. Check glucose when appropriate.
E — Exposure
Measure temperature and examine the abdomen and relevant areas while maintaining privacy and preventing hypothermia.

content_groups.group_title: Immediate actions in a seriously unwell patient

items.text: Call for senior emergency, gynaecological and surgical assistance as appropriate.
Establish two large-bore IV cannulas if major haemorrhage or shock is suspected.
Send urgent blood tests, including full blood count, blood group and crossmatch when indicated.
Begin appropriate fluid and blood-product resuscitation according to the clinical condition and local protocol.
Provide analgesia and antiemetics.
Keep the patient nil by mouth if urgent surgery is possible.
Arrange urgent imaging or operative assessment without delaying definitive treatment.

blocks.text: Take a targeted history while the patient is being assessed and treated.

“Good morning. My name is … I understand you are experiencing pain in your lower abdomen. I would like to ask a few questions about the pain, your menstrual and pregnancy history, and any other symptoms. Because some causes of pelvic pain need urgent treatment, I will also assess your vital signs and arrange any necessary investigations. Is that alright?”
If the patient is critically unwell, immediate stabilization takes priority over formal introductions and a complete history.

rows: Is the pain central, right-sided, left-sided or generalized?
Did it begin suddenly or gradually?
Is it sharp, cramping, stabbing, burning or dull?
Does it spread to the shoulder tip, back, groin or thighs?
Vomiting, fever, bleeding, discharge, urinary or bowel symptoms?
Is it constant, intermittent or cyclical?
Does movement, intercourse, urination or defecation worsen it?

blocks.text: Clarify whether the pain is worsening, whether it has happened before and whether the patient has taken any medication.

items.text: Date of the last menstrual period.
Regularity and length of cycles.
Recent missed periods.
Heavy or abnormal bleeding.
Dysmenorrhoea.
Intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding.

blocks.text: A missed period or irregular menstruation does not exclude pregnancy, and bleeding does not exclude ectopic pregnancy.

items.text: Is there any possibility that you could be pregnant?
Are you using contraception?
Have you taken a pregnancy test?
Have you previously had an ectopic pregnancy?
Have you had pelvic inflammatory disease, tubal surgery or fertility treatment?
What is your obstetric history?

blocks.text: Important: Perform a pregnancy test whenever pregnancy is biologically possible, regardless of reported contraception use.
Gynaecological

items.text: Vaginal bleeding or discharge.
Pain during sexual intercourse.
Recent sexually transmitted infection risk.
Previous ovarian cysts, endometriosis or fibroids.

blocks.text: Gastrointestinal

items.text: Nausea or vomiting.
Loss of appetite.
Diarrhoea or constipation.
Abdominal distension.
Passage of blood in stool.

blocks.text: Urinary

items.text: Dysuria.
Frequency or urgency.
Haematuria.
Flank pain.
Difficulty passing urine.

blocks.text: Systemic

items.text: Fever or chills.
Dizziness or syncope.
Weakness, pallor or breathlessness.

blocks.text: When relevant, ask sensitively about sexual activity, contraception, sexually transmitted infection exposure and safety at home. Explain confidentiality and obtain permission before discussing sensitive details.

content_groups.group_title: G. Past medical and surgical history

items.text: Previous abdominal or pelvic surgery.
Ectopic pregnancy.
Pelvic inflammatory disease.
Endometriosis or ovarian cysts.
Bleeding disorders.
Anticoagulant use.
Allergies and regular medications.

rows: Possible pregnancy, pelvic pain, vaginal bleeding, shoulder-tip pain or collapse
Sudden unilateral pain, often with nausea and vomiting
Sudden pelvic pain; possible free fluid or internal bleeding
Pelvic pain, discharge, fever, cervical motion tenderness
Often right lower abdominal pain, anorexia, nausea and evolving tenderness
Positive pregnancy test, cramping and vaginal bleeding
Severe flank pain radiating to groin, possible haematuria
Dysuria, frequency, fever or flank pain
Localized pain, known fibroid, sometimes pregnancy
Alternative acute causes must be excluded
Previous cyclical pain, dysmenorrhoea or deep dyspareunia

blocks.text: Urine or serum β-hCG is a key early investigation in patients who could be pregnant.
A negative urine test may be insufficient in very early pregnancy or when clinical suspicion remains high; serum testing may be appropriate.

items.text: Full blood count.
Blood group, Rh status and crossmatch when relevant.
Urea, electrolytes and renal function.
CRP where it may help assess inflammation.
Blood cultures and lactate if sepsis is suspected.
Coagulation studies when indicated.
Additional tests guided by the differential diagnosis.

blocks.text: No normal blood test reliably excludes ectopic pregnancy, torsion or appendicitis.
Urinalysis may identify blood, leukocytes or nitrites, but abnormal findings must be interpreted in context. Urinary abnormalities do not necessarily exclude a gynaecological cause.
Transvaginal ultrasound is often preferred for gynaecological assessment when appropriate and acceptable. Transabdominal ultrasound may be added.

items.text: The uterus and endometrial cavity.
Ovaries and adnexa.
Adnexal masses.
Free fluid or suspected haemoperitoneum.
Pregnancy location when relevant.
Features suggestive of torsion or tubo-ovarian abscess.
A very early intrauterine pregnancy may not yet be visible.
Normal Doppler flow does not exclude ovarian torsion.
Free fluid may be physiological or pathological; interpretation depends on volume, appearance and clinical findings.
Imaging should not delay emergency surgery when the patient is unstable.
CT abdomen/pelvis: May be appropriate when appendicitis, urinary stones or another abdominal diagnosis is suspected, taking pregnancy status into account.
MRI: May be useful in selected stable patients, particularly in pregnancy when ultrasound is inconclusive and further imaging is needed.

blocks.text: Scenario 1: A woman has pelvic pain, a positive pregnancy test and an empty uterus on ultrasound.

Interpretation: This is a pregnancy of unknown location unless the scan establishes a diagnosis. Ectopic pregnancy must be considered. Assess clinical stability, ultrasound findings and quantitative β-hCG trends, with urgent specialist management according to symptoms and findings.
Scenario 2: A woman has severe unilateral pain, vomiting and an enlarged ovary with peripheral follicles.
Interpretation: Ovarian torsion is a major concern. Urgent gynaecological assessment is required even if Doppler flow is preserved.
Scenario 3: A woman has fever, pelvic pain, purulent discharge and cervical motion tenderness.
Interpretation: Pelvic inflammatory disease is likely, but assess for pregnancy-related emergencies, tubo-ovarian abscess and other causes of acute abdominal pain.
Recognize: Pelvic pain, possible pregnancy, vaginal bleeding, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness or collapse.

items.text: Assess ABCDE and haemodynamic stability.
Obtain urgent gynaecological review.
Perform pregnancy testing, quantitative β-hCG and pelvic ultrasound as appropriate.
If ruptured ectopic pregnancy or significant haemorrhage is suspected, initiate resuscitation and arrange urgent surgical management.
In a stable patient, management may include expectant care, methotrexate or surgery, depending on clinical findings, ultrasound, β-hCG, eligibility and follow-up reliability.

blocks.text: Do not delay emergency management of a suspected ruptured ectopic pregnancy while waiting for serial β-hCG results.
Recognize: Sudden unilateral pelvic pain, often with nausea and vomiting.

items.text: Provide analgesia and assess stability.
Obtain urgent gynaecological review.
Perform ultrasound with Doppler if it does not delay care.
Arrange urgent laparoscopy when clinically indicated.
Detorse the ovary and preserve ovarian tissue where feasible.

blocks.text: Normal Doppler flow does not rule out torsion.

content_groups.group_title: C. Ruptured or haemorrhagic ovarian cyst

blocks.text: Recognize: Sudden pelvic pain, sometimes with free pelvic fluid.

items.text: Assess haemodynamic stability and pregnancy status.
Obtain blood tests, including haemoglobin, and crossmatch if significant bleeding is suspected.
Provide analgesia and monitor stable patients with reassuring findings.
Escalate urgently for persistent instability, significant haemoperitoneum or ongoing bleeding; surgery may be necessary.

blocks.text: Recognize: Pelvic pain, vaginal discharge, cervical motion tenderness and sometimes fever.

items.text: Assess for pregnancy, sepsis and tubo-ovarian abscess.
Obtain appropriate STI testing and other investigations.
Start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics according to current local guidance when PID is suspected.
Arrange inpatient treatment for severe illness, pregnancy, suspected abscess, inability to tolerate oral medication or failure of outpatient treatment.

blocks.text: Recognize: Often progressive right lower abdominal pain, anorexia, nausea and localized tenderness, although presentation varies.

items.text: Assess stability and provide analgesia.
Request appropriate blood tests and pregnancy testing.
Obtain surgical review and suitable imaging.
Treat with surgery or another evidence-based pathway according to diagnosis, severity and local protocol.

blocks.title: For suspected UTI, pyelonephritis or renal colic:

items.text: Perform urinalysis and urine culture when indicated.
Assess renal function and signs of systemic infection.
Use appropriate imaging when obstruction or stones are suspected.
Treat infection and pain according to severity and local guidance.

blocks.text: “A reproductive-age woman presents with acute lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. Pregnancy status is not yet established. My priority is to assess haemodynamic stability and perform a pregnancy test. If positive, I would arrange urgent pelvic ultrasound and gynaecological review to assess for ectopic pregnancy. If she is unstable or rupture is suspected, I would initiate resuscitation and arrange emergency definitive management.”

“A woman presents with sudden severe right-sided pelvic pain and vomiting. Examination reveals localized right lower abdominal tenderness. My leading differential is ovarian torsion, although ectopic pregnancy, a ruptured ovarian cyst and appendicitis must also be considered. I would provide analgesia, assess vital signs, perform pregnancy testing and arrange urgent gynaecological review. Ultrasound with Doppler may support the diagnosis, but normal flow would not exclude torsion.”

“A woman presents with lower abdominal pain, fever and abnormal vaginal discharge. Pelvic examination demonstrates cervical motion tenderness. These findings are suggestive of pelvic inflammatory disease. I would assess for pregnancy, sepsis and tubo-ovarian abscess, obtain appropriate microbiological tests and commence empiric antibiotics according to local guidance.”

“A woman presents with sudden pelvic pain, pallor, tachycardia and hypotension. This is a potentially life-threatening presentation consistent with haemodynamic compromise. I would initiate ABCDE resuscitation, obtain intravenous access, request urgent blood tests and crossmatching, and involve senior emergency and gynaecological teams. Ectopic pregnancy and haemorrhage from a ruptured ovarian cyst are key differentials. I would not delay definitive management for routine imaging.”

content_groups.group_title: Example 5 — Stable patient with undifferentiated pelvic pain

blocks.text: “The patient is haemodynamically stable and has lower abdominal tenderness without generalized peritonism. I would take a focused menstrual, pregnancy, urinary and gastrointestinal history, perform an appropriate examination, obtain a pregnancy test and arrange targeted investigations. My differential includes ovarian cyst complications, ectopic pregnancy, PID, appendicitis and urinary pathology.”
Explain to the patient:

“Pain in the lower abdomen can come from the reproductive organs, urinary tract or bowel. Some causes are minor, but others, such as an ectopic pregnancy or twisted ovary, require urgent treatment. We need to assess your vital signs, check whether you could be pregnant and perform the appropriate investigations.
“We will provide pain relief while investigating the cause. If we find evidence of a condition requiring urgent surgery or other treatment, we will explain the findings and next steps to you.”

For a patient discharged after an appropriate assessment, give clear return precautions for worsening pain, fainting, heavy bleeding, fever, persistent vomiting or new concerning symptoms. Discharge should only occur when the clinical assessment supports it and an appropriate follow-up plan is in place.

subsections.subsection_title: 11. Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the first priority in acute pelvic pain?
Assess haemodynamic stability using ABCDE and identify conditions requiring immediate intervention.
Q2. Which investigation is essential when pregnancy is possible?
A pregnancy test, with quantitative serum β-hCG when indicated.
Q3. Name three time-critical gynaecological diagnoses.
Ruptured ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion and significant haemorrhage from a ruptured ovarian cyst. Severe PID with sepsis or tubo-ovarian abscess can also be urgent.
Q4. Does a negative urine pregnancy test always exclude pregnancy?
Not in every circumstance. Very early pregnancy or strong clinical suspicion may require serum testing and further assessment.
Q5. What is the significance of shoulder-tip pain?
It may reflect diaphragmatic irritation from intraperitoneal blood and is concerning in a patient with possible ectopic pregnancy or intra-abdominal haemorrhage.
Q6. What are the features of PID?
Pelvic or lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness, uterine or adnexal tenderness, abnormal discharge and sometimes fever. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by investigations.
Q7. Does normal Doppler flow exclude ovarian torsion?
No. Urgent assessment remains necessary when the clinical suspicion is high.
Q8. When is urgent surgical referral indicated?
When there is suspected ectopic pregnancy with rupture, ovarian torsion, significant intra-abdominal haemorrhage, peritonitis or another surgical emergency.
Q9. What are the major non-gynaecological differentials?
Appendicitis, renal colic, UTI, pyelonephritis, bowel obstruction and gastrointestinal inflammation.
Q10. What should you do if the patient is unstable?

Call for urgent help, initiate resuscitation, establish IV access, obtain urgent blood tests and crossmatch as appropriate, and expedite definitive management without waiting for routine investigations.

items.text: Taking a full routine history before checking vital signs.
Forgetting pregnancy testing.
Assuming vaginal bleeding excludes ectopic pregnancy.
Assuming normal Doppler flow excludes torsion.
Failing to consider appendicitis and urinary causes.
Delaying resuscitation while waiting for imaging.
Giving antibiotics without considering the likely diagnosis and local guidelines.
Discharging without a clear diagnosis, appropriate follow-up or safety-net advice.

blocks.text: PAIN — initial assessment

items.text: P — Pregnancy test.
A — Assess ABCDE and vital signs.
I — Investigate urgent gynaecological and surgical causes.
N — Notify senior teams and do not delay emergency care.

blocks.text: E-T-A-P — must-not-miss diagnoses

items.text: E — Ectopic pregnancy.
T — Torsion of the ovary.
A — Appendicitis.
P — Pelvic inflammatory disease and haemorrhage from a ruptured cyst.

blocks.text: Remember that this is a memory aid, not a substitute for a complete differential diagnosis.
1. A 27-year-old woman with acute pelvic pain is pale, hypotensive and tachycardic. What should you do first?
Wait for pelvic ultrasound
Perform a detailed sexual history
Begin ABCDE assessment and emergency resuscitation while calling for help
Give oral analgesia and discharge
2. A woman has pelvic pain, vaginal bleeding and a positive pregnancy test. Which diagnosis must be excluded urgently?
PCOS
Ectopic pregnancy
Uncomplicated fibroids
Vaginal candidiasis
3. Which statement about suspected ovarian torsion is correct?
Normal Doppler flow excludes torsion
Surgery should wait until Doppler flow disappears
Normal Doppler flow does not exclude torsion
Torsion only occurs when an ovarian cyst is present
4. A woman presents with fever, lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge and cervical motion tenderness. What is the leading diagnosis?
Pelvic inflammatory disease
Ovarian cancer in every case
Uncomplicated renal colic
Normal ovulation
5. Which symptom may indicate intraperitoneal bleeding in a patient with pelvic pain?
Mild acne
Shoulder-tip pain with dizziness or collapse
Long-standing hirsutism
Isolated chronic constipation
